claims.text: Nanoparticles containing five or more metals in near-equimolar ratios can initially crystallize as a single-phase solid solution.
High configurational entropy counteracts the tendency of these nanoparticles to undergo phase separation.
Rapid atomic diffusion promotes local chemical inhomogeneity and phase separation.
Entropy-stabilized multielement nanoparticles can exhibit high diffusion barriers and sluggish kinetics.
Sluggish atomic kinetics can preserve a uniform elemental distribution during thermal annealing.
Greater diffusion equilibration can produce segregation, particularly for selected constituent elements.
The relative diffusion rates of individual metals govern local chemical ordering and the onset of phase separation.
A minor alloying addition or surface treatment can specifically slow the fastest-diffusing constituent.
Slowing the fastest-diffusing constituent will preserve a homogeneous solid solution better than an unmodified control.
The diffusion-modified nanoparticles will show minimal phase and chemical-distribution changes relative to their initial solid-solution state.
Unmodified or diffusion-enhanced nanoparticles will exhibit earlier phase separation or intermetallic formation.
The proposed entropy-versus-diffusion stabilization mechanism applies throughout 473–1923 K.
The baseline nanoparticles are initially uniform in structure and composition.
Controlling atmosphere, particle size, ramp rate, dwell time, and thermal cycling limits extrinsic differences between modified and control samples.
The quantitative diffusion-rate threshold and temperature at which entropy stabilization ceases to dominate are not established.
A lack of measurable segregation or phase-stability difference between samples with demonstrably different diffusion rates would falsify the proposed causal role of diffusion modification.

contradictions.description: The proposal calls for an alloying addition or surface treatment while also saying that overall composition or otherwise identical nanoparticles will be maintained. An alloying addition changes elemental composition, and a surface treatment changes surface chemistry, unless a compensating substitution and the meaning of 'identical' are explicitly defined.
